title: Air Inter 148 (Mont Sainte-Odile)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Rapport de la Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident survenu le 20 janvier 1992 près du Mont Sainte-Odile (Bas-Rhin) à l'Airbus A320 immatriculé F-GGED exploité par la compagnie Air Inter

location.name: La Bloss ridge near Mont Sainte-Odile, Vosges, Bas-Rhin

summary: On a night VOR/DME approach to Strasbourg runway 05, after a late change of runway and approach by ATC, the crew descended from the final approach fix at about 3,300 ft/min instead of the intended 3.3 degree flight path angle. The aircraft struck the wooded ridge of La Bloss at 2,620 ft in cloud. 87 of the 96 occupants died; the wreckage was not located for several hours.
probable_cause: The Commission concluded that the accident was most probably due to a very high rate of descent during the final approach, the origin of which could not be determined with certainty; the most probable hypothesis was that the crew selected a vertical speed of -3,300 ft/min when they intended a flight path angle of -3.3 degrees on the FCU, whose display of the two modes was similar. Contributing factors included the crew's high workload following the late change of approach, the absence of cross-checking of the descent, the absence of a GPWS on the aircraft, the lack of an altitude check-call culture at Air Inter, and the limited radar and MSAW coverage at Strasbourg.

factors.evidence: ATC changed the expected ILS approach to runway 23 to a VOR/DME approach to runway 05 late in the descent, requiring the crew to re-plan under time pressure.
The crew were re-briefing the approach, managing the autopilot and flying a tight circuit with little time between the approach fix and the descent.
The most probable hypothesis is that the crew set -33 on the FCU in vertical speed mode (-3,300 ft/min) while intending -3.3 degrees flight path angle.
The FCU display presented flight path angle and vertical speed in a similar two-digit format with only a small mode indication, facilitating confusion.
Neither pilot monitored the vertical speed or altitude against the approach profile during the roughly one-minute descent.
There was no callout or cross-check of altitude and descent rate between the two pilots.
The aircraft was not fitted with a GPWS; Air Inter had obtained an exemption, so no terrain warning was available to the crew.
Air Inter had chosen not to equip its fleet with GPWS and did not require altitude callouts on non-precision approaches.
Strasbourg approach radar did not provide minimum safe altitude warning to the controller.
The approach was flown at night in cloud with no visual reference to the terrain.
The aircraft was in cloud with snow showers over the Vosges during the descent.
The aircraft struck the ridge at 2,620 ft in a controlled descent with no indication that the crew saw the terrain.

events.text: Flight IT148 departs Lyon for Strasbourg with 90 passengers and 6 crew; the captain is pilot flying.
Strasbourg approach informs the crew that the ILS to runway 23 is not available for them and offers a VOR/DME approach to runway 05; the crew re-brief the approach.
ATC vectors the aircraft to intercept the final approach track, which brings it to the ANDLO final fix closer in than planned.
The crew set up the descent on the FCU; the most probable hypothesis is a -33 selection in vertical speed mode rather than -3.3 degree flight path angle.
Aircraft begins descent from about 5,000 ft after ANDLO at about 3,300 ft/min, well above the expected 800 ft/min.
Controller, without MSAW, sees nothing abnormal on the radar and clears the crew to continue; no altitude alert is available.
The aircraft passes through 3,500 ft in cloud at night still descending at high rate; no callouts are made and no GPWS is fitted.
Aircraft strikes trees on the ridge of La Bloss at 2,620 ft in level flight and breaks up; 87 of 96 occupants die.
Rescuers reach the wreckage some four hours after the accident; nine survivors are recovered.

recommendations.text: Make the carriage of a ground proximity warning system mandatory on French public transport aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: GPWS became mandatory in France and Air Inter equipped its fleet.

recommendations.text: Modify the FCU so that the vertical speed and flight path angle modes are clearly distinguishable in the display.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus modified the FCU display to show vertical speed with four digits and flight path angle with two digits and a decimal point.

recommendations.text: Extend minimum safe altitude warning coverage at French approach radar facilities and review approach procedures at Strasbourg.
Introduce systematic altitude and descent rate callouts and cross-checks during non-precision approaches.
Improve the location of accident sites through ELT performance and coordination of search and rescue.

safety_changes: GPWS made mandatory in France; Air Inter equipped its A320 fleet.
Airbus FCU display modification distinguishing V/S from FPA (four digits versus two with decimal point).
Reinforced altitude callouts and approach monitoring procedures at Air Inter and improved SAR coordination.

notes: Impact at 18:20:33 UTC (19:20 local) is from the report; intermediate times and the descent initiation clock are approximate.
The ATC runway change and radar vectoring are recorded contributors but the report attributes the descent rate primarily to the probable FCU mode confusion, which could not be proved definitively.
Report reference number omitted; recommendation ids null.
